missingStrategy.mostFrequent: Fill with the most common value

missingHelp.none: Leaves blanks as they are. A column with even one blank cannot be used for training.
missingHelp.drop: Leaves out of training any row with a blank cell. You end up with less data to train on.
missingHelp.mean: Fills blanks with the column's average. In a lopsided column the average can sit far from most of the values.
missingHelp.median: Fills blanks with the middle value when the column is sorted by size. Unusually large or small values (outliers) affect it less.
missingHelp.mostFrequent: Fills blanks with the value that appears most often. It also works on text columns.
missingHelp.zero: Fills blanks with 0. If 0 already means something in that column, the filled zeros can no longer be told apart from the real ones.

scalingHelp.none: Uses the values as they are. When columns have different units, the one with bigger numbers counts for more. Height in cm next to weight in kg is such a case.
scalingHelp.standard: Subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, giving mean 0 and variance 1. It suits values close to a normal (bell-shaped) distribution and is the most widely used.
scalingHelp.minmax: Maps values into 0 to 1 using the smallest and largest value. Good when the range is fixed, but a single outlier squeezes the rest into a narrow range.
scalingHelp.robust: Rescales values using the median and the interquartile range. Outliers affect it less.

encodingBasis.onehot: One-hot encoding → {count} column | One-hot encoding → {count} columns

encodingHelp.none: Leaves text values alone. Models take numbers only, so columns that hold text are left out of training.
encodingHelp.onehot: Makes one column per distinct value and puts 1 in the matching one. Use it when the values have no order. Many distinct values means that many new columns.
encodingHelp.ordinal: Numbers the distinct values 0, 1, 2 and so on. No new columns, but the model reads those numbers as sizes, so use it only when the values have an order, such as grades A, B, C.

client.SVM_NOT_CONVERGED: The decision boundary was not fully adjusted within the maximum number of iterations. The scores are real, but the model has not converged yet. Choose a method under [Scaling] in the preprocessing step, or lower [Inverse of regularization strength (C)], and the boundary is easier to find.
client.LOGISTIC_NOT_CONVERGED: The best fit was not reached within the maximum number of iterations. The scores are real, but the model has not converged yet. Choose a method under [Scaling] in the preprocessing step and it converges in far fewer iterations. If the same notice appears, raise [Maximum iterations (maxIter)] in the training step.
client.NEURAL_NOT_CONVERGED: All the epochs ran, but the model has not converged yet. The scores are real, but the model is not fully trained. The loss curve on the results screen shows whether the loss was still going down. To raise the scores, try choosing a method under [Scaling] in the preprocessing step.
client.NEURAL_REGRESSION_NOT_CONVERGED: The loss did not reach the point where it stops going down within the set number of epochs. The scores are real, but the model is not fully trained. The loss curve on the results screen shows whether the loss was still going down. This notice is common when the target values are much larger than the feature values.
client.TARGET_TOO_FEW_CLASSES: The data used for training has only one target value, so the model had nothing to tell apart. A high score here does not mean it learned anything. On the preprocessing screen, choose a target column that has two or more values. ({value})
client.TARGET_NO_VARIANCE: Every target value in the training data is the same, so R-squared cannot be calculated meaningfully. Judge by the error scores (RMSE, MAE), or choose a target column whose values vary. ({value})

metricHelp.accuracy: The share of all samples the model got right. It is easy to understand, but when one class holds most of the data it makes the model look better than it is. For example, if 90 of 100 samples share one class, answering with that class every time already scores 90%. Read it together with the other scores.
metricHelp.f1: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, so a high score on only one of them does not lift it. For example, 90% precision with 10% recall gives an F1 score of 18%. It is worked out for each class, and this model’s F1 score is the average of those.
metricHelp.precision: Of the samples the model predicted as this class, the share that really were this class. What matters is the denominator: the number of samples the model predicted as this class. For example, in a factory test it asks how many of the parts judged faulty really were faulty. A low number means the model picks this class too often and flags good parts as faulty.
metricHelp.recall: Of the samples that really are this class, the share the model found. The denominator is the number of samples that really are this class, and that is what separates it from precision. For example, in a factory test it asks how many of the truly faulty parts were caught, because the ones missed ship out. Missing a class (recall) and picking it too often (precision) are different problems, so read the two together.
metricHelp.specificity: Of the samples that are not this class, the share the model correctly judged as not this class. For example, in a medical test it is the ability to tell a healthy person they are healthy, and when it is low, more healthy people are wrongly told they are ill. It is easy to confuse with precision: both relate to the mistake of calling something this class when it is not, but precision divides by the number the model predicted as this class while specificity divides by the number of samples that truly are not this class.
metricHelp.support: How many samples of this class the test data used for evaluation really held. It is not the number used for training. When it is small, the scores beside it change a lot from small differences. For example, when it is 3, getting one more right or wrong moves recall by 33 points.
metricHelp.r2: How much of the variation in the values the model explains. Closer to 1 is better. 0 means it did no better than always predicting the average regardless of the input, and anything worse goes negative.
metricHelp.rmse: How far the predictions land from the real values, and lower is better. Errors are squared before they are averaged, so one badly wrong prediction pushes the number up a long way. The unit is the same as the value being predicted: if you predicted a price in dollars, read this in dollars.
metricHelp.mae: How far the predictions land from the real values on average, and lower is better. Every error carries the same weight, so one badly wrong prediction affects it less. For example, if everything else is close but a single prediction is far off, RMSE climbs sharply while this number rises only a little.
metricHelp.silhouette: How well each sample fits its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster, averaged over every sample. It runs from -1 to 1, and the closer to 1, the more clearly the clusters are separated. Around 0 the cluster boundaries touch each other, and a negative score means many samples are closer to another cluster than to their own.
metricHelp.inertia: The squared distance from every sample to the centroid of its own cluster, all added up. Lower means tighter clusters, but it always drops as you add more clusters, so it cannot tell you on its own whether the result is good. For example, record the value with 2, 3, and 4 clusters and look for the point where the drop suddenly becomes small.

columnHelp.target: The column the model has to guess. You can pick only one, and the column you pick cannot also be a feature. For example, to guess exam scores, the score column is the target. Clustering has no target.
columnHelp.feature: A column the model uses as evidence. You can pick several, and columns you leave unpicked are not used in training. For example, to guess exam scores you might pick study hours and attendance.
columnHelp.kind: Whether this column was automatically judged as Numeric or Categorical from its data. Numeric columns go through scaling, categorical ones through encoding. Some columns are written as numbers but their size has no meaning, such as a grade level or a postal code, so it is worth checking for yourself.
columnHelp.missing: How many rows have no value here. Empty cells must be either filled in or left out before training, and you choose which in [Data cleaning] below.
columnHelp.unique: How many different values this column holds. A column with only one value cannot tell any data apart, so it does not help training, and a categorical column adds one encoded column per value, so many values means many columns.
columnHelp.effect: What actually happens to this column with the current settings. Filled-in values and scaling are worked out from the training data only, so these numbers are not the whole column.

boundary.lead: Each point on the plane formed by the two features is shaded with the category the model predicts there. Dots are the actual categories of the test data. A dot on a background of another color is a row the model predicted wrongly.

importance.title: Permutation importance
importance.lead: The values of one column of the test data were randomly shuffled across rows, the drop in score was measured {count} times, and the average is shown. A longer bar means the model relies more on that column when predicting. A value near zero or below means the column barely affects this model's predictions. Two columns that carry similar information can both come out low, because shuffling one leaves the other to take its place.
importance.baseline: Measured against the score of {score} before shuffling.
importance.mismatch: The new predictions do not match the saved score, so the permutation importance is not drawn.
